n: Now the priests—Aaron’s descendants—are organized into divisions. The chapter starts with Aaron’s four sons.
Nadab and Abihu died without children after offering unauthorized fire, so the priesthood passed through Eleazar and Ithamar.

f.w: Nadab and Abihu died before their father

n: David works with Zadok (from Eleazar’s line) and Ahimelech (from Ithamar’s line) to organize the priests.

f.w: Zadok of the sons of Eleazar
Ahimelech of the sons of Ithamar

n: Eleazar’s line had more family heads, so it received sixteen divisions and Ithamar’s eight—twenty-four in all.

f.g: Sixteen family heads, each leading a priestly division.

n: The divisions were assigned by lot so that both families shared equally in honor, since both had produced leaders of the sanctuary. Lots left the choice to God and prevented favoritism.
A Levite scribe, Shemaiah, officially recorded the drawing before the king and leaders, alternating between Eleazar’s and Ithamar’s families. Careful records ensured fairness and order.

f.g: Recorded the results in front of witnesses.

n: The first lot fell to Jehoiarib and the second to Jedaiah. Each division served in the temple for a week at a time, in rotation.
The third and fourth divisions.
The fifth and sixth divisions.
The eighth division belonged to Abijah. Centuries later, the priest Zacharias, father of John the Baptist, served in this course when the angel Gabriel appeared to him.
The ninth and tenth divisions; Jeshua was a common priestly name after the exile.

f.g: A form of Joshua—the same name as Jesus.

n: The eleventh and twelfth divisions.
The thirteenth and fourteenth divisions.

f.g: A priestly division mentioned only here.

n: The fifteenth and sixteenth divisions, including Immer’s, whose descendant Pashur struck Jeremiah.
The seventeenth and eighteenth divisions.

f.g: A family name later carved on a priestly tomb in Jerusalem’s Kidron Valley.

n: The nineteenth and twentieth divisions.

f.g: The same name as Ezekiel, “God strengthens.”

n: The twenty-first and twenty-second divisions.

f.g: Also the name of one of the temple’s two bronze pillars (1 Kings 7:21).

n: The twenty-third and twenty-fourth divisions complete the list. This system of twenty-four courses was still in use in New Testament times.
Each division came to the temple in its turn according to the pattern God gave Aaron. Order in worship reflects the God of order.

f.w: as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him

n: The chronicler now lists the remaining Levite family heads, updating the list from chapter 23 by a generation.
Rehabiah’s branch, descended from Moses, was led by Isshiah.
The Izharites, led by Shelomoth and his son Jahath.
Hebron’s four leaders are repeated from the earlier list.
Uzziel’s branch through Michah and his son Shamir.
Michah’s brother Isshiah and his son Zechariah.
The Merarites, including a branch through Jaaziah not listed earlier.
Jaaziah’s descendants are named.

f.g: May mean “his son” rather than a name.

n: Mahli’s son Eleazar had no sons.
Kish’s son Jerahmeel headed his own division.

f.g: A Levite; not the Judahite Jerahmeel of chapter 2.

n: Mushi’s sons close the list of Levite family heads.
The Levites also cast lots for their duties, just like the priests, with senior and junior families treated alike. In God’s service, rank did not decide one’s place.

f.w: the principal fathers over against their younger brethren
f.g: The heads of the senior families were treated the same as the junior ones.
